passage:
Liam had told three people why he'd dropped out of the Tuesday Spanish class in Dublin: the bus timetable was awful, the teacher moved too fast, and with work, who had the energy? The reasons sounded solid every time.
On Sunday, tidying his desk, he found the course book and, half as a joke, wrote the reasons on a sticky note. Then he asked himself: if Yosef said this to me, would I buy it? He crossed out the bus; there was one every ten minutes. He crossed out the teacher. Underneath he wrote the real reason: "I felt stupid when I couldn't answer in front of everyone." One short line, and not flattering.
He texted Yosef, who had signed up with him: "Actually, I quit because I was embarrassed. Could we practise together before class?"

qa.q: What did Liam first write on the sticky note?
qa.a: His reasons for dropping the class: the bus timetable, the teacher moving too fast, and having no energy after work.

qa.q: Why had the long list of reasons felt convincing to Liam?
qa.a: They protected him from feeling embarrassed; the real reason, feeling stupid in front of everyone, was less flattering and harder to admit.

qa.q: What made Liam's test work?
qa.a: Imagining Yosef giving the same excuses made the weak ones obvious, and the honest one-line reason pointed to a real fix: practising together 🙂.

qa.q: How might Yosef react to Liam's text?
qa.a: Yosef may feel trusted and glad to help, and might find it easier to admit his own struggles in class too.

grounding: An adult writes down the reasons for a choice, tests them as if a friend gave them, and finds the short, unflattering real reason.

passage:
The monsoon had turned the Kolkata lanes into rivers the week Dadu died. At the prayer meeting in the flat, relatives cried in corners, but Sunaina sat straight on the sofa and explained things to her cousin Pranav in a level voice.
"It was heart failure. The muscle gets weak, fluid builds up in the lungs, that's why he was so breathless. It's actually very common at his age. The doctors said the last stage can move fast."
Pranav nodded, unsure. "Sunaina, are you okay?"
"I'm fine. I read about it last night." She went on about oxygen levels.
Two days later, finding Dadu's reading glasses in the fruit bowl, she sat down on the kitchen floor and finally cried.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say Dadu died of?
qa.a: Heart failure.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina talk about medical details in such a level voice?
qa.a: Sunaina felt deep grief underneath, and thinking about the facts kept the pain at arm's length so she could stay composed.

qa.q: How could Pranav support Sunaina?
qa.a: Sit with her, let her talk about the facts if she needs to, and gently say it is okay to be sad whenever the tears come, perhaps sharing a memory of Dadu.

qa.q: What was it like for Pranav to hear the medical explanation?
qa.a: He felt unsure and worried, because the calm facts did not match the crying around them, so he asked whether she was okay.

grounding: A teenager whose grandfather has died recites medical facts in a flat voice, and the tears come only days later.

subtype: Analysing a breakup like a case study [Actor]
passage:
Counselling note, the Friday before the Christmas break.
Abhinav came in with a notebook. He had drawn two circles with arrows, "anxious" for himself and "avoidant" for his ex, and a loop between them. He spoke fluently for twenty minutes about attachment styles and why the relationship "was structurally doomed". His roommate Deepak, who walked him over, had told me Abhinav had not eaten in the mess all week.
When I asked, "And how did the last evening feel?" Abhinav said, "Feelings aren't really useful data here," and turned to another diagram. His knee bounced the whole time.
Next: I have offered a second session after the break, and I will begin by asking about his week, not the theory.

qa.q: What did Abhinav draw in his notebook?
qa.a: Two circles with arrows, labelled anxious and avoidant, and a loop between them.

qa.q: Why might Abhinav keep turning to diagrams?
qa.a: He seems deeply hurt, and analysing the breakup lets him feel in control while keeping the pain at a distance; his bouncing knee hints at the tension.

qa.q: What does the counsellor plan, and why might it help?
qa.a: Beginning next time with how his week went, not the theory, gently invites the feeling in while still respecting his thinking.

qa.q: How does Deepak seem affected by Abhinav's breakup?
qa.a: Deepak is worried enough to walk him over and mention he has not been eating, showing he sees more than the calm analysis.

grounding: A student explains his breakup through diagrams and theory while avoiding how it felt, as a counsellor notices.

subtype: Letting thinking and feeling share the table [Response]
passage:
Yusuf: saw your status. so sorry about Bruno
Chetan: thanks. been reading about it all morning
Chetan: kidney trouble in old dogs is really common, the vet said he was fourteen
Chetan: I made a timeline of his last month. now it makes sense why he stopped eating
Yusuf: that sounds like you
Yusuf: does it help?
Chetan: it did. I get what happened. no mystery
Chetan: but I noticed I'm doing it so I don't have to think about him asleep on my bed
Chetan: so I'm going to stop reading

Chetan: Amma is sending old videos of him. I'll watch them tonight, properly. probably cry
Yusuf: want company? I'll bring chai at 9
Chetan: yes. thank you, really

qa.q: What did Chetan make about Bruno's last month?
qa.a: A timeline of his last month.

qa.q: Why did Chetan decide to stop reading?
qa.a: Chetan noticed the research, though useful, was keeping the sadness at arm's length, and felt ready to let the grief for Bruno in.

qa.q: Which approach works here, and why?
qa.a: Using analysis to understand what happened, then setting a time to watch the videos and actually feel it, with Yusuf there, lets understanding lead towards the feeling.

qa.q: How does Yusuf respond to Chetan's way of coping?
qa.a: Yusuf gently asks whether it helps instead of judging, then offers company and chai at nine so Chetan does not grieve alone.

grounding: A student uses analysis to understand the loss of a dog and then sets aside time to feel it.

subtype: Partner wants feelings and gets a lecture [Receiver]
passage:
The power had gone out across the colony in the May heat, and their flat was lit by one phone torch. Himani finally said it: "I was hurt you didn't come to the opening last night."
Aadhya set down her glass of water and began, calmly. "Okay, but look at it logically. One, I told you last week the audit might run late. Two, the exhibition runs for two weeks, so I haven't missed the art. Three, your parents were there, so you weren't alone."
Each point was true. Himani fanned herself with a newspaper and felt her throat tighten. "I know all that," she said. "I didn't want reasons. I wanted you to say you're sorry you missed it."
Aadhya opened her mouth to answer point one again, then stopped.

qa.q: What were Aadhya's three points?
qa.a: The audit might run late, the exhibition runs for two weeks, and Himani's parents were there.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling as Aadhya listed the points?
qa.a: Himani felt unheard and hurt, her throat tightening, because true reasons were answering a feeling that wanted an apology.

qa.q: What could Aadhya say instead?
qa.a: Something like "I'm sorry I missed it; I can see it hurt" before any explanation, and perhaps plan to visit the exhibition together.

qa.q: Why might Aadhya respond with logic?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel guilty or defensive, and explaining feels like the way to fix things; stopping mid-sentence suggests she is starting to see it is not working.

grounding: Someone who says she is hurt gets a well-argued case for why the hurt is illogical, and feels unheard though every point is correct.

subtype: Noticing the calm that rings hollow [Observer]
passage:
Usha had exactly fifteen minutes before her train, so she met Sumit at the noisy station food court. He had been laid off on Monday, along with half his team.
"Honestly, it makes sense," he said over the announcements. "Funding dried up, our product line was the least profitable, restructuring was inevitable. I'd have done the same."
He talked as if presenting a slide. But his tea sat untouched, his eyes were red-rimmed, and he mentioned, almost proudly, that he'd been up till three updating his CV three nights running.
Usha put her hand flat on the table between them. "I believe you understand why it happened, Sumit. I'm asking something else. How does it feel?"
He stared at the tea for a long moment. "Like I wasn't worth keeping," he said quietly.

qa.q: How long did Usha have before her train?
qa.a: Exactly fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What made Usha concerned despite Sumit's calm explanation?
qa.a: Usha felt concerned because the untouched tea, red-rimmed eyes and late nights did not match his smooth reasoning; the calm seemed hollow.

qa.q: Why was Usha's question a wise choice?
qa.a: By accepting his understanding and asking how it feels, she opened the door to the hurt his analysis was covering; she could check in again after her trip.

qa.q: How does Sumit experience the layoff underneath the analysis?
qa.a: He feels he was not worth keeping, a painful sense of rejection that his tidy reasons had kept hidden.

grounding: A mentor sees a junior talk about a layoff in rational terms while skipping food and sleep, and asks how it feels.

subtype: Excessive kindness to a resented rival [Actor]
passage:
In the week before Ganesh Chaturthi, when the school corridors were crowded with clay idols from art class, a new boy named Divyansh joined Class 5B and got the seat next to Kunal, Mridul's best friend.
By Wednesday, Mridul was everywhere Divyansh was. He carried Divyansh's bag, shared his whole tiffin and announced loudly, "Divyansh is my best friend now!" He laughed a little too hard at every joke. When Kunal and Divyansh sat together to paint their Ganpati, Mridul squeezed in between them, grinning. "I'll help you both!"
At home that evening he slammed his art box shut and said nothing about school.

qa.q: What did Mridul carry for Divyansh?
qa.a: Divyansh's bag.

qa.q: Why did Mridul keep announcing that Divyansh was his best friend?
qa.a: He felt jealous and pushed aside when Divyansh took the seat next to Kunal, and loud friendliness hid a feeling he could not admit.

qa.q: How could a parent help Mridul?
qa.a: Gently ask about the new boy and Kunal, and let Mridul say he feels left out without being told off, so he does not need to act so hard.

qa.q: What might it be like for Divyansh to have Mridul follow him everywhere?
qa.a: He may feel welcomed but also a bit crowded and puzzled, sensing the friendliness is too much.

grounding: A child who feels displaced by a new classmate becomes loudly sweet and clingy towards him, masking jealousy.

subtype: Mocking the one who is liked [Actor]
passage:
Dear Lalremsiami (Siami!),
Merry Christmas! Is Aizawl all lights and carols? Here in Shillong it's freezing and everyone is just exams, exams.
Okay, confession. You know Ashwin, from the debate team? At the Christmas fair yesterday he wore this huge red sweater, and I shouted in front of everyone, "Look, it's Santa's tomato!" Everyone laughed. Then I kept going, about his hair, his squeaky voice. I don't even think his voice is squeaky.
Here's the weird part. I actually like talking to him. A lot. Maybe that's why I did it? If I make fun of him, nobody can tell I like him, not even him. But he looked really hurt.
What do I do? Tell no one.
Love,
Ritu

qa.q: What did Ritu shout at the Christmas fair?
qa.a: "Look, it's Santa's tomato!"

qa.q: Why did Ritu mock Ashwin in front of everyone?
qa.a: Ritu likes Ashwin and felt afraid of being exposed, so teasing him loudly hid the crush from everyone, even from him.

qa.q: What could Ritu do now?
qa.a: Apologise to Ashwin simply, without jokes, and next time just talk to him normally, even while feeling shy 😅.

qa.q: How might Ashwin have felt at the fair?
qa.a: He probably felt embarrassed and hurt, and confused, since Ritu usually enjoys talking to him.

grounding: A teenager with a crush loudly mocks the boy in front of friends, the opposite behaviour protecting against feeling exposed.

subtype: Fierce scorn for a secret temptation [Actor]
passage:
It was Margazhi season in Chennai, and every sabha was packed. In the hostel common room, Lakshmi mentioned that a senior had quit engineering to study Carnatic music full time. Indu put her tea down so hard it spilled.
"That's so selfish. Her parents paid for three years, and now she'll sing at weddings? People like that just want attention."
Lakshmi blinked. "You sound really angry about someone you've never met."
"Because it's irresponsible," Indu snapped, and went back to her room.
She had left the door open. Lakshmi saw, under the bed, the old veena Indu never mentioned, its cover freshly dusted. That night Lakshmi heard her humming a varnam, very softly, until nearly midnight.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi see under Indu's bed?
qa.a: The old veena Indu never mentioned, its cover freshly dusted.

qa.q: What might Indu's strong anger about the senior suggest?
qa.a: Her anger is far bigger than the situation, hinting that she is secretly drawn to music herself and feels envious or torn about a path she did not take.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi respond wisely?
qa.a: Avoid confronting Indu about the veena; later, gently ask whether she still plays, leaving room for her to talk.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see Indu's outburst?
qa.a: Lakshmi is surprised and puzzled, noticing the anger is too strong for someone Indu has never met.

grounding: A young adult condemns a senior's switch to music with unusual heat while secretly keeping and humming music herself.

passage:
When I got the team-lead role in April, Jahnavi was the first to congratulate me. Then the second, and the fifth. She posted about it on the team channel, brought a cake with "Our Star Parveen" in blue icing, and told every visiting client, "Parveen is simply the best, honestly the best."
By the third week it felt odd. We'd both applied. She had wanted it at least as much as I had. I caught myself wondering whether it was all a performance, or a trap.
Looking back, I think it was simpler: she was trying very hard to be generous while something else ached. That doesn't make her an enemy. I stopped reading so much into the cake and asked her to co-lead the June launch with me. She hesitated, then said yes, and the gushing slowly quietened.

qa.q: What was written on Jahnavi's cake?
qa.a: "Our Star Parveen" in blue icing.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling by the third week of praise?
qa.a: Parveen felt uneasy and a little suspicious 🤔, wondering whether the praise was a performance, before settling on a kinder reading.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Not treating the excess as proof of ill will, and inviting Jahnavi to co-lead the launch, gave her a real role and let the tension ease.

qa.q: What might the promotion have been like for Jahnavi?
qa.a: She had wanted it too, so she likely felt disappointed while trying hard to be generous; the gushing may have covered that ache.

grounding: A colleague notices a rival's excessive praise of a promotion and reads it as mixed feelings rather than ill will.
